25896.content:
serverless workloads are becoming increasingly blurred, and new trends are emerging that redefine what
orchestration really means in modern computing.
Serverless containers
One of the most i d x _ 4 6 3 9 5 4 8 b significant developments in recent years is the convergence of container orchestration and
serverless computing. Traditional orchestration platforms are excellent at keeping long-running services available,
but many modern workloads are event-driven and short-lived. Serverless container offerings such as AWS Fargate,
Google Cloud Run, and Azure Container Apps combine the flexibility of containers with the elasticity of serverless
execution.
In these models, you still package your application as a container, but you no longer manage any nodes or clusters.
The underlying orchestration layer scales the container instances automatically based on demand, even down to
zero when idle. This shift enables organizations to focus purely on application logic rather than infrastructure,
while still benefiting from the consistency and portability of containers.

GitOps and declarative management
Another i d x _ 2 4 8 d 4 9 c 3 strong trend is the adoption i d x _ 5 6 e 0 0 7 2 6 of GitOps principles in orchestration. GitOps extends Kubernetes' declarative
model by introducing version control and continuous delivery practices to the infrastructure itself. With Git as the
single source of truth, every change to a cluster, whether it's a deployment, a configuration update, or a policy
change, is represented as a commit.
Tools such i d x _ d e c 4 d f 1 9 as Argo CD and Flux watch i d x _ 8 1 2 2 0 d 5 a these repositories and automatically reconcile the running system with the
declared state. This approach improves auditability, enables full rollback through Git history, and brings
infrastructure management closer to standard software engineering workflows. In many organizations, GitOps has
become the operational backbone of modern platform engineering.
Multi-cluster and edge orchestration
As applications i d x _ 6 2 b c 3 c c d increasingly span multiple regions and environments, orchestration must extend beyond a single
cluster. Multi-cluster orchestration allows workloads to be deployed, observed, and managed consistently across
hybrid or multi-cloud setups. Kubernetes federation and tools such i d x _ 2 4 4 8 b 4 e e as KubeFed, Anthos, and Azure Arc provide i d x _ 4 f 1 8 3 e 1 9
this layer of control, enabling unified policy i d x _ d 6 b 8 4 0 c c enforcement and workload placement across many clusters.
At the same time, edge computing is reshaping orchestration at the opposite end of the spectrum. Lightweight
Kubernetes distributions i d x _ 3 b 3 c 8 b 6 0 such i d x _ 9 8 2 f 5 6 d 9 as K3s, MicroK8s, and k0s make it feasible to run fully i d x _ 4 2 1 a e f 6 5 functional clusters on small
form-factor devices or embedded systems. These edge clusters can synchronize with centralized control planes,
enabling workloads to run close to the data they process, which is a crucial capability for IoT and low-latency
applications.
AI-driven scheduling and optimization
With the i d x _ 9 f 4 3 f 2 3 3 rise of data-intensive and machine learning workloads, orchestration systems are being extended to
support AI-assisted scheduling and resource optimization. New components, such as Kubernetes' Kueue or i d x _ 6 5 d 5 e 4 3 7 the
Cluster Autoscaler with predictive scaling, leverage telemetry data and machine learning models to anticipate
demand and optimize placement.
These intelligent schedulers can make dynamic decisions about where and when to run workloads based on
performance, cost, or energy efficiency. Over time, this will lead to more autonomous orchestration systems that
continuously learn and adapt to real-world usage patterns without requiring manual tuning.
Security and policy as code
As i d x _ f 5 0 d 7 8 6 3 orchestration becomes the foundation of enterprise infrastructure, security and compliance have become first-

25898.title: ultimatedockercontainerbookfourthedition
25898.heading: Chapter 14 468
25898.content:
class citizens. Modern i d x _ 0 3 d b c 4 4 e clusters increasingly integrate policy-as-code frameworks such as Open Policy Agent (OPA)
and Kyverno, allowing i d x _ e 2 3 8 d 2 3 0 teams to enforce governance and security rules declaratively.
These policies i d x _ 5 a 2 f 5 1 4 7 can validate configurations, restrict network access, or ensure images originate from trusted
registries, all before a workload is deployed. Combined with initiatives such i d x _ 1 c 7 f f e e 1 as Software Bills of Materials
(SBOMs) and the Supply-chain Levels for Software Artifacts (SLSA) framework, orchestration i d x _ 8 3 4 a e 7 9 9 platforms are
now playing a key role in maintaining end-to-end software supply chain integrity.
469 Introducing Container Orchestration
Abstracted platforms and developer experience
Finally, as i d x _ 1 4 f 4 b 7 b 4 orchestration technology matures, there is a growing movement to hide its complexity behind i d x _ 1 4 5 0 5 a d 4 higher-
level i d x _ 3 c b 2 2 6 1 f developer platforms. Internal developer portals such as Backstage, Port, or Humanitec offer i d x _ 1 5 8 d 3 5 4 7 user-friendly
interfaces that allow engineers to deploy and monitor applications without having to interact directly with
Kubernetes.
This evolution marks a shift from infrastructure-centric to developer-centric orchestration. The focus is no longer
solely on managing clusters, but on delivering a friction-free developer experience where provisioning
environments, deploying services, and applying policies are self-service, secure, and automated.
This evolution aligns closely with the principles i d x _ f b 4 c 3 a b 3 of platform engineering, where orchestration becomes a behind-
the-scenes capability that powers internal developer platforms.
Summary
In this chapter, we learned why container orchestrators have become indispensable for running distributed
applications reliably at scale. We discovered how orchestrators continuously reconcile a system's desired state with
its actual state, ensuring that workloads remain healthy, responsive, and correctly distributed across the available
nodes.
We explored the key responsibilities of an orchestrator, ranging from scheduling and service discovery to scaling,
self-healing, and secure configuration management. We also reviewed the most prominent orchestration
platforms and their typical use cases. Kubernetes clearly stands out as the dominant standard, supported by all
major cloud providers and surrounded by a thriving ecosystem of tools and extensions. Lighter alternatives such as
Docker Swarm and HashiCorp Nomad, however, still serve well in scenarios where simplicity or mixed workloads
matter more than ecosystem depth.
Finally, we looked at the emerging trends that are shaping the future of orchestration. Serverless containers,

GitOps automation, policy as code, AI-driven scheduling, and internal developer platforms all point toward an era
where orchestration becomes increasingly autonomous, secure, and developer-friendly.
In the next chapter, we will take a closer look at Kubernetes, the orchestrator that has redefined how modern
systems are deployed and operated. We will explore its architecture, its core building blocks, and how it enables
developers and operators to run highly available, self-healing, and scalable applications both in the cloud and on-
premises.

Introducing Kubernetes
In this chapter, you will learn how Kubernetes—the industry-standard container orchestrator—automates the
deployment, scaling, and management of containerized applications. You will explore its architecture and core
building blocks, set up a local cluster using Docker Desktop, minikube, or kind, and learn how to deploy and
observe workloads in action. Finally, you will discover key ecosystem tools such as GitOps, Helm 3, and Kustomize,
which bring automation, consistency, and simplicity to modern Kubernetes operations.
In the previous chapter, Chapter 14, Introducing Container Orchestration, we explored how orchestrators simplify the
complex task of running distributed, containerized applications at scale. We learned how they reconcile the
desired and actual state of a system, perform scheduling, service discovery, and scaling, and even apply self-healing
and security mechanisms automatically. By now, you should have a solid understanding of what an orchestrator
does and why it has become indispensable for modern software systems.
It is now time to look i d x _ e 5 0 3 f 0 2 5 more closely at the orchestrator that has redefined the industry standard: Kubernetes.
Originally developed at Google and later donated i d x _ 1 7 d 9 f 7 b 9 to the Cloud Native Computing Foundation (CNCF),
Kubernetes is today the most widely adopted orchestration platform. It embodies many of the concepts we
discussed earlier—declarative management, self-healing, and desired-state reconciliation—and extends them
with an exceptionally rich ecosystem and extensible architecture.
In this chapter, we will explore how Kubernetes works under the hood. We will start by looking at its high-level
architecture and understanding the roles of the control plane and the worker nodes. You will learn about the key
components of the system—such as the API Server, Controller Manager, Scheduler, and the etcd data store—and
how they collaborate to maintain the cluster's desired state.
We will then move to the practical side and learn how to run Kubernetes locally using lightweight options such as
Docker Desktop, minikube, or kind (Kubernetes in Docker). These tools make it easy to experiment with
Kubernetes on your own machine before deploying workloads to a cloud provider. You will set up your first cluster,
deploy simple workloads, and observe how Kubernetes manages and exposes them through its built-in
abstractions.
From there, we will gradually introduce the fundamental building blocks of Kubernetes: Pods, ReplicaSets,
Deployments, and Services. Each of these plays a distinct role in defining how applications are packaged,
replicated, updated, and made accessible within the cluster. Understanding these concepts is essential for

25913.title: ultimatedockercontainerbookfourthedition
25913.heading: Chapter 20, Real-World Containerization Patterns
25913.content:
mastering Kubernetes, as nearly every higher-level construct builds on top of them.
Finally, we will look beyond the basics and explore popular tools and practices that have grown around Kubernetes
—specifically GitOps, Helm 3, and Kustomize. These tools bring automation, configuration management, and
reproducibility to the next level. They enable teams to treat their cluster configurations and deployments as
version-controlled artifacts, making it easier to scale and manage complex systems reliably.
After reading and practicing the exercises in this chapter, you will be able to do the following:
Explain the high-level architecture of Kubernetes, including the roles of control-plane and worker nodes
Describe what a Kubernetes Pod is and how it differs from a standalone container
Define and deploy ReplicaSets, Deployments, and Services to manage and expose your applications
Run a local Kubernetes cluster using Docker Desktop, minikube, or kind
Deploy a sample application to your cluster and inspect how Kubernetes maintains its desired state
Understand how modern tools such as GitOps, Helm 3, and Kustomize simplify deployment automation
and configuration management
With this knowledge, you will not only be able to deploy applications into Kubernetes but also truly understand
what happens behind the scenes—how the system maintains health, scales workloads, and enforces the
declarative model that makes cloud-native operations possible.
Let's begin our deep dive into Kubernetes—the orchestrator that has become the backbone of today's cloud-native
world.
Technical requirements
To follow along with the examples in this chapter, you need a working Docker environment and one or more local
Kubernetes options installed. All examples can be executed on macOS, Windows, or Linux. You will primarily work
with the command line and use kubectl, the official Kubernetes command-line interface.
Make sure that you have the following software installed and running on your system:
Docker Desktop (latest version): Includes a fully functional, single-node Kubernetes cluster i d x _ 4 1 1 9 f 8 2 7 that can be
enabled through its settings panel. It also installs the kubectl CLI automatically.
kubectl (if not installed via Docker Desktop): The command-line tool used to interact with i d x _ 8 f 9 4 8 7 6 5 Kubernetes
clusters. You can verify its installation with the following:

To prepare your working environment, navigate to the folder where you cloned the book's sample repository and
create a subfolder for this chapter:
$ cd ~/The-Ultimate-Docker-Container-Book-Fourth-Edition

https://github.com/PacktPublishing/The-Ultimate-Docker-Container-Book-Fourth-Edition
Now that we have our environment ready, let's dive into the details of Kubernetes and how to use it.
Understanding Kubernetes architecture
A Kubernetes cluster i d x _ 0 1 9 0 8 0 4 f consists of a set of servers. These servers can be VMs or i d x _ a 8 7 8 e 0 f e physical servers. The latter is also
i d x _ 0 e f e c 4 3 5 called bare metal. Each member of the cluster can have one of two roles. It is either a Kubernetes master or a
(worker) node. The former is used to manage the cluster, while the latter will run an application workload. I have
put worker in parentheses since, in Kubernetes parlance, you only talk about a node when you're talking about a
server that runs application workloads. But in Docker and Swarm parlance, the equivalent is a worker node. I think
that the notion of a worker node better describes the role of the server than a simple node.
In a cluster, you have a small and odd number of masters and as many worker nodes as needed. Small clusters
might only have a few worker nodes, while more realistic clusters might have dozens or even hundreds of worker
nodes. Technically, there is no limit to how many worker nodes a cluster can have, though you might experience a
significant slowdown in some management operations when dealing with thousands of nodes.
On the Kubernetes worker nodes, we run Pods. This is a new concept not present in Docker or Docker Swarm. A
Pod is the atomic unit of execution on a Kubernetes cluster. In many cases, a Pod i d x _ 5 2 f 6 2 6 e 5 contains a single container, but a
Pod can consist of many containers running co-located. We will describe Pods in much more detail later in this
section.
All members of the cluster need to be connected by a physical network, the so-called underlay network. Kubernetes
defines one flat network for the whole cluster. Kubernetes does not provide any networking implementation out of
the box. Instead, it relies on plugins from third parties.
Kubernetes just defines i d x _ 0 2 8 f b c 2 9 the Container Network Interface (CNI) and leaves the implementation to others. The
CNI is pretty simple. It states that each Pod running in the cluster must be able to reach any other Pod also running
in the cluster without i d x _ 2 4 6 0 4 6 8 e any Network Address Translation (NAT) happening in between. The same must be true
between cluster nodes and Pods—that is, applications or daemons running directly on a cluster node must be able

25916.title: ultimatedockercontainerbookfourthedition
25916.heading: Chapter 15 476
25916.content:
to reach each Pod in the cluster, and vice versa.
The following diagram i d x _ 5 e c 1 0 1 8 f illustrates the high-level architecture of a Kubernetes cluster:
477 Introducing Kubernetes
Figure 15.1 – High-level architecture diagram of Kubernetes
The i d x _ 9 d 3 6 b 5 0 9 preceding diagram is explained as follows:
In the top box, in the middle, we have a cluster of etcd nodes. An etcd node i d x _ 5 a d f 3 0 5 3 is a distributed key-value store that, in
a Kubernetes cluster, is used to store all the states of the cluster. The number of etcd nodes has to be odd, as
mandated by the Raft consensus protocol, which states which nodes are used to coordinate among themselves.
When we talk about the cluster state, we do not include data that is produced or consumed by applications
running in the cluster. Instead, we're talking about all the information on the topology of the cluster, what services
are running, network settings, secrets used, and more. That said, this etcd cluster is i d x _ 3 3 2 a 9 2 1 a mission-critical to the overall
cluster, and thus, we should never run only a single etcd server i d x _ 2 6 e 0 a d 7 f in a production environment or any environment
that needs to be highly available.
Then, we have a cluster of Kubernetes master nodes, which also form a consensus group among themselves,
similar to i d x _ 5 7 1 8 7 9 9 7 the etcd nodes. The number of master nodes also has to be odd. We can run clusters with a single
master, but we should never do that in a production or mission-critical system. There, we should always have at
least three master nodes. Since the master nodes are used to manage the whole cluster, we are also talking about
the management plane.

Master nodes i d x _ 7 8 c a b f 1 c use the etcd cluster as their backing store. It is good practice to put a load balancer (LB) in i d x _ e 6 7 b 3 b b 8 front of
master nodes with a i d x _ e 1 d 8 5 5 c e well-known Fully Qualified Domain Name (FQDN), such as https://admin.example.com.
All tools that are used to manage the Kubernetes cluster should access it through this LB rather than using the
public IP address of one of the master nodes. This is shown on the upper-left side of the preceding diagram.
Toward the bottom of the diagram, we have a cluster of worker nodes. The number of nodes can be as low as one
and does not have an upper limit.
Kubernetes master and worker nodes communicate with each other. It is a bidirectional form of communication
that is different from the one we know from Docker Swarm. In Docker Swarm, only i d x _ a 3 f 5 0 3 1 d manager nodes communicate
with worker nodes and never the other way around. All ingress traffic accessing applications running in the cluster
should go through another LB.
This is the i d x _ 8 8 a 3 5 2 c a application LB or reverse proxy. We never want external traffic to directly access any of the worker
nodes.
Now that we have an idea about the high-level architecture of a Kubernetes cluster, let's delve a bit more deeply
and look at the Kubernetes master and worker nodes.
Kubernetes master nodes
Kubernetes master nodes i d x _ 3 9 8 3 d c 6 6 are used to manage a Kubernetes cluster. The following is a high-level diagram of such a
master:
Figure 15.2 – Kubernetes master
479 Introducing Kubernetes
At the bottom of the preceding i d x _ 6 7 8 0 0 4 2 4 diagram, we have the infrastructure, which can be a VM, on-premises or in the
cloud, or a server (often called bare metal) on-premises or in the cloud.
Currently, Kubernetes masters only run on Linux. The most popular Linux distributions, such as RHEL, CentOS,
and Ubuntu, are supported. On this Linux machine, we have at least the following four Kubernetes services
running:
API server: This is the gateway to Kubernetes. All requests to list, create, modify, or delete any resources
in i d x _ f 0 e 3 1 4 7 0 the cluster must go through this service. It exposes a i d x _ 5 f b e c 7 9 e REST interface that tools such as kubectl can use
to manage the cluster and applications in the cluster.
Controller: The controller, or i d x _ 7 4 4 d 9 e c d more precisely the controller manager, is a control loop that observes i d x _ 2 2 b 2 9 9 0 2 the
state of the cluster through the API server and makes changes, attempting to move the current or
effective state toward the desired state if they differ.
Scheduler: The scheduler i d x _ a 9 e 2 d f 6 d is a service that tries its best to schedule Pods on worker i d x _ 0 c 0 b e c b d nodes while
considering various boundary conditions, such as resource requirements, policies, quality of service

25918.heading: Chapter 15 478
25918.content:
requirements, and more. The scheduler first filters nodes that meet the pod's requirements and then
scores the remaining nodes to choose the best placement.
Cluster store: This is an i d x _ 7 f 3 7 7 f 4 d instance of etcd that is used to store all information about the i d x _ 4 8 d b 2 8 7 6 state of the
cluster. To be more precise, etcd, which is used as a cluster store, does not necessarily have to be installed
on the same node as the other Kubernetes services. Sometimes, Kubernetes clusters are configured to use
standalone clusters of etcd servers, as shown in Figure 15.1. But which variant to use is an advanced
management decision and is outside the scope of this book.
We need at least one master, but to achieve high availability, we need three or more master nodes.
Kubernetes masters never run i d x _ b 6 1 5 3 9 5 7 application workloads. Their sole purpose is to manage the cluster. Kubernetes
masters build a Raft consensus group. The Raft protocol i d x _ 0 d 8 3 3 5 d 4 is a standard protocol used in situations where a group of
members needs to make decisions. It is used in many well-known software products such as MongoDB, Consul
(HashiCorp), and Kubernetes.

How the control plane collaborates
Although the control-plane components are separate processes, they cooperate through a shared
control loop centered around the API server and etcd. Every component interacts with the cluster
exclusively through the API server. When a user or automation tool submits a resource definition
—such as a Pod or Deployment—the API server stores this desired state in etcd. Controllers
continuously watch the API server for changes and attempt to reconcile the current state with the
desired state. The scheduler then assigns newly created Pods to suitable worker nodes. Finally,
the kubelet on each node observes the assigned workload and instructs the container runtime to
start or stop containers accordingly. Through this continuous feedback loop, Kubernetes
automatically drives the system toward the declared desired state.

As we mentioned in the previous section, the state of the Kubernetes cluster is stored in an etcd node. If the
Kubernetes cluster is supposed to be highly available, then the etcd node must also be configured in HA mode,
which normally means that we have at least three etcd instances running on different nodes.
Let's state once again i d x _ 1 f d f 9 6 d e that the whole cluster state is stored in an etcd node. This includes all the information about
all the cluster nodes, all the replica sets, Deployments, secrets, network policies, routing information, and so on. It
is therefore crucial that we have a robust backup strategy in place for this key-value store.
Now, let's look at the nodes that will be running the actual workload of the cluster.
Cluster nodes
Cluster nodes are the nodes i d x _ 8 a 2 3 e b 4 5 with which Kubernetes schedules application workloads. They are the workhorses of
the cluster. A Kubernetes cluster can have a few, dozens, hundreds, or even thousands of cluster nodes. Kubernetes
has been built from the ground up for high scalability. Don't forget that Kubernetes was modeled on Google Borg,
which has been running tens of thousands of containers for years:
Figure 15.3 – Kubernetes worker node
A worker node (which is a cluster node, as are the master nodes) can run on a VM, bare metal, on-premises, or in
the cloud. Originally, worker nodes could only be configured on Linux, but since i d x _ f 4 1 0 3 c 7 d version 1.10 of Kubernetes, worker

At times, specifically in development and test scenarios, it can make sense to work with a single-node
Kubernetes cluster, which then naturally becomes a master and a worker node at the same time. But this
scenario should be avoided in production.

nodes can also run on Windows Server 2010 or later. It is perfectly fine to have a mixed cluster with Linux and
Windows worker nodes.
On each node, we have three services that need to run, as follows:
Kubelet: This is the first and foremost service. Kubelet is the primary node agent. The Kubelet i d x _ 0 d 7 3 6 7 1 7 service
uses Pod specifications to make sure all of the containers of the corresponding Pods are running and
healthy. Pod specifications are files written in YAML or JSON format, and they declaratively describe a
Pod. We will get to know what Pods are in the next section. PodSpecs is provided to Kubelet primarily
through the API server.
Container runtime: The second service that needs to be present on each worker node is a container
runtime. Kubernetes, by default, has used containerd since version 1.9 as its container i d x _ f 2 5 3 0 1 1 7 runtime. Prior to
that, it used the Docker daemon. Other container runtimes, such as rkt or CRI-O, can be used. The
container runtime is responsible for managing and running the individual containers of a Pod.

kube-proxy: Finally, there is i d x _ 3 1 f 3 4 e e 9 the kube-proxy. It runs as a daemon and is a simple network proxy and LB
for all application services running on that particular node.
Now that we have learned about the architecture of Kubernetes and the master and worker nodes, it is time to
introduce the tooling that we can use to develop applications targeted at Kubernetes.

Before deploying applications to a i d x _ b 3 4 3 c c a 8 production-grade Kubernetes cluster, it is essential to first experiment in a safe
and local environment. Fortunately, Kubernetes can be run directly on your laptop or workstation using
lightweight distributions that behave just like a real cluster. These local setups are ideal for learning, testing, and
rapid development because they provide the same APIs, configuration model, and command-line tools as their
cloud-based counterparts.
In this section, we will i d x _ d c 5 2 a d b 5 explore the most i d x _ 6 6 a e 2 e 0 1 common options for running Kubernetes locally: Docker Desktop,
minikube, and kind. Each of them has its own strengths, and together they i d x _ d 8 3 8 a 8 3 7 cover nearly every learning and
development scenario you might encounter.

Introduction to Pods
Contrary to what is possible with Docker Compose and Docker Swarm, you cannot run containers directly in a

such as the network namespace. No equivalent exists in Docker Swarm. The fact that more than one container can

illustrates two Pods:

Ethernet (veth) endpoint. The first container gets veth0, the next one gets veth1, and so on. These virtual Ethernet

Traffic is routed from the docker0 bridge to every connected veth endpoint. Every container has its own network

For a Kubernetes i d x _ 0 7 f 9 d 9 5 9 Pod, the situation is i d x _ 0 f 1 b 8 c b 9 different. When creating a new Pod, Kubernetes first creates a so-called pause

Other than that, it does nothing useful; it is just sleeping. The pause container is connected to the docker0 bridge
through veth0. Any subsequent container that will be part of the Pod uses a special feature of the Docker engine
that allows it to reuse an existing network namespace. The syntax to do so looks like this:

Pod life cycle
Earlier in this book, we learned i d x _ 7 e 8 f 5 a f 3 that containers have a life cycle. A container is initialized, run, and ultimately
exited. When a container exits, it can do this gracefully with an exit code zero, or it can terminate with an error,
which is equivalent to a non-zero exit code.
Similarly, a Pod has a life cycle. Because a Pod can contain more than one container, this life cycle is slightly more
complicated than that of a single container. The life cycle of a Pod can be seen in the following diagram:
Figure 15.12 – The life cycle of Kubernetes Pods
When a Pod is i d x _ e f 2 e 3 5 5 5 created on a cluster node, it first enters the pending status. Once all the containers of the Pod are up
and running, the Pod enters the running status. The pod only enters this state if all its containers run successfully. If
the Pod is asked to terminate, it will request all its containers to terminate. If all containers terminate with exit code
zero, then the Pod enters the succeeded status. This is the happy path.
Now, let's look at some scenarios that lead to the Pod being in a failed state. There are three possible scenarios:
If, during the startup of the Pod, at least one container is not able to run and fails (that is, it exits with a
non-zero exit code), the Pod goes from the pending state into the failed state
If the Pod is in the running state and one of the containers suddenly crashes or exits with a non-zero exit
code, then the Pod transitions from the running state into the failed state
If the Pod is i d x _ 6 7 5 7 8 6 8 4 asked to terminate and, during the shutdown, at least one of the containers exits with a non-
zero exit code, then the Pod also enters the failed state
Now, let's look at the specifications for a Pod.

25932.content:

In general, the declarative approach is strongly preferred in all established orchestrators, and Kubernetes is no
exception.
Thus, in this chapter, we will exclusively concentrate on the declarative approach. Manifests or specifications for a
Pod can be written using either the YAML or JSON formats. In this chapter, we will concentrate on YAML since it is
easier to read for us humans. Let's look at a sample specification. Here is the content of the pod.yaml file, which can
be found in the ch15 subfolder of our labs folder:
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
name: web-pod
spec:
containers:
- name: web
image: nginx:alpine
ports:
- containerPort: 80
Each specification in Kubernetes starts with the version information. Pods have been around for quite some time,
and thus, the API version is v1. The second line specifies the type of Kubernetes object or resource we want to
define. Obviously, in this case, we want to specify a Pod. Next follows a block containing metadata. At a bare
minimum, we need to give the Pod a name. Here, we call it web-pod. The next block that follows is the spec block,
which contains the specification of the pod. The most important part (and the only one in this simple sample) is a
list of all containers that are part of this Pod. We only have one container here, but multiple containers are possible.
The name we chose for our container is web, and the container image is nginx:alpine. Finally, we define a list of
ports the container is exposing.

25942.content:
Chapter 15 498
Now that we have a good understanding of Pods, let's investigate how those Pods are managed with the help of
ReplicaSets.
Kubernetes ReplicaSet
A single Pod in an environment with high availability requirements is insufficient. What if the Pod crashes? What if
we need to update the application running inside the Pod, but cannot afford any service interruption? These
i d x _ 8 a 5 6 2 0 a e questions and more indicate that Pods alone are not enough, and we need a higher-level concept that can manage
multiple instances of the same Pod. In Kubernetes, the ReplicaSet is used to define and manage such a collection of
identical Pods that are running on different cluster nodes. Among other things, a ReplicaSet defines which
container images are used by the containers running inside a Pod and how many instances of the Pod will run in
the cluster. These properties and many others are called i d x _ 9 9 2 d c 9 9 2 the desired state.
The ReplicaSet is i d x _ 8 3 c c 7 8 5 9 responsible for reconciling the desired state at all times if the actual state ever deviates from it.
Here is a Kubernetes ReplicaSet:
Figure 15.15 – Kubernetes ReplicaSet
In the preceding diagram, we can see a ReplicaSet that governs a number of Pods. The Pods are called pod-api. The
ReplicaSet is responsible for making sure that, at any given time, there is always the desired number of Pods
running. If one of the Pods crashes for whatever reason, the ReplicaSet schedules a new Pod on a node with free
resources instead. If there are more Pods than the desired number, then the ReplicaSet kills superfluous Pods. With
this, we can say that the ReplicaSet guarantees a self-healing and scalable set of Pods. There is no limit to how
many Pods a ReplicaSet can hold.
ReplicaSet specification
Similar to what we i d x _ 8 e 2 a f 5 5 3 have learned about Pods, Kubernetes also allows us to either imperatively or declaratively
define and create a ReplicaSet. Since the declarative approach is by far the most recommended one in most cases,
we're going to concentrate on this approach. Let's work with a sample specification for a Kubernetes ReplicaSet:
Create a new file called replicaset.yaml and add the following content to it:
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: ReplicaSet
metadata:
name: rs-web
spec:

25943.title: ultimatedockercontainerbookfourthedition

25943.content:
1.499 Introducing Kubernetes
selector:
matchLabels:
app: web
replicas: 3
template:
metadata:
labels:
app: web
spec:
containers:
- name: nginx
image: nginx:alpine
ports:
- containerPort: 80
This looks an awful lot like the Pod specification we introduced earlier. Let's concentrate on the
differences, then. First, on line 2, we have the kind, which was a Pod, and is now ReplicaSet. Then, on
lines 6–8, we have a selector, which determines the Pods that will be part of the ReplicaSet. In this case, it
is all the Pods that have app as a label with the web value. Then, on line 9, we define how many replicas of
the Pod we want to run—three, in this case. Finally, we have the template section, which i d x _ 6 7 b 5 f e a 4 first defines the
metadata, and then the spec, which defines the containers that run inside the Pod. In our case, we have a
single container using the nginx:alpine image and exporting port 80.
The really important elements are the number of replicas and the selector, which specifies the set of Pods
governed by the ReplicaSet.
Let's use this file to create the ReplicaSet:
$ kubectl apply -f replicaset.yaml
This results in the following:

Now, we list all the ReplicaSets in the cluster (rs is a shortcut for ReplicaSet):

We get the following:

Kubernetes Deployments
Kubernetes takes the single-responsibility i d x _ 4 6 2 2 6 5 d 0 principle very seriously. All Kubernetes objects are designed to do one
thing and one thing only, and they are designed to do this one thing very well. In this regard, we must understand
Kubernetes ReplicaSets and Deployments. A ReplicaSet, as we have learned, is responsible for achieving and
reconciling the desired state of an application service. This means that the ReplicaSet manages a set of Pods.
A Deployment augments i d x _ e 3 1 e c e e 5 a ReplicaSet by providing rolling updates and rollback i d x _ d c 7 d 6 2 5 2 functionality on top of it. In
Docker Swarm, the Swarm service incorporates the functionality of both ReplicaSet and Deployment. In this
regard, SwarmKit is much more monolithic than Kubernetes. The following diagram shows the relationship of a
Deployment to a ReplicaSet:

Figure 15.17 – Kubernetes Deployment
In the preceding diagram, the ReplicaSet defines and governs a set of identical Pods. The main characteristics of the
ReplicaSet are that it is self-healing, scalable, and always does its best to reconcile the desired state. A Kubernetes
Deployment, in turn, adds rolling updates and rollback functionality to this. In this regard, a Deployment is a
wrapper object for a ReplicaSet.
We will learn more about rolling updates and rollbacks in Chapter 16, Deploying, Updating, and Securing an

In the next section, we will learn more about Kubernetes services and how they enable service discovery and
routing.
Kubernetes Services
The moment i d x _ d 5 d 2 2 c a d we start to work with applications consisting of more than one application service, we need service
discovery. The following diagram illustrates this problem:
Figure 15.18 – Service discovery
In the preceding diagram, we have a Web API service that needs access to three other services: payments, shipping,
and ordering. The Web API service should never have to care about how and where to find those three services. In
503 Introducing Kubernetes
the API code, we just want to use the name of the service we want to reach and its port number. A sample would be
http://payments:3000, which is used to access an instance of the payments service.
In Kubernetes, the payments application service is represented by a ReplicaSet of Pods. Due to the nature of highly
distributed systems, we cannot assume that Pods have stable endpoints. A Pod can come and go on a whim. But
that's a problem if we need to access the corresponding application service from an internal or external client. If we
cannot rely on Pod endpoints being stable, what else can we do?
This is i d x _ b c 0 5 1 8 3 5 where Kubernetes Services come into play. They are meant to provide stable endpoints to ReplicaSets or
Deployments, as follows:
Figure 15.19 – Kubernetes service providing stable endpoints to clients
In the preceding diagram, in the center, we can see such a Kubernetes Service. It provides a reliable cluster-wide IP
address, also called i d x _ 2 8 0 5 0 d 7 9 a virtual IP (VIP), as well as a reliable port that's unique in the whole cluster. The Pods that the
Kubernetes Service is proxying are determined by the selector defined in the service specification. Selectors are
always based on labels. Every Kubernetes object can have zero or many labels assigned to it. In our case, the
selector is app=web; that is, all Pods that have a label called app with a value of web are proxied.

Figure 15.25 – Context-based routing using a Kubernetes ingress controller
In the preceding diagram, we i d x _ 5 6 7 5 a 4 5 6 can see how context-based (or layer 7) routing works when using an ingress
controller, such as NGINX. Here, we have the Deployment of an application service called web. All the Pods of this
application service have the following label: app=web. Then, we have a Kubernetes Service called web that provides a
stable endpoint to those Pods. The Service has a (virtual) IP of 52.14.0.13 and exposes port 30044. That is, if a
request comes to any node of the Kubernetes cluster for the name web and port 30044, then it is forwarded to this
Service. The Service then load balances the request to one of the Pods.
So far, so good, but how is an ingress request from a client to the http[s]://example.com/web URL routed to our
web service? First, we must define routing from a context-based request to a corresponding <service name>/
<port> request. This is done through an Ingress object:
In the Ingress object, we define the host and path as the source and the (service) name, and the port as
the target. When this Ingress object is created by the Kubernetes API server, then a process that runs as a

Popular tools: GitOps, Helm 3, and Kustomize
By now, you should have a good understanding of Kubernetes' core concepts—how it manages Pods, ReplicaSets,
Deployments, and Services to keep applications running in a desired state. In practice, however, managing all those
YAML manifests manually can quickly become tedious. As your application grows, you might end up maintaining
dozens or even hundreds of configuration files across multiple environments such as development, staging, and
production.
To handle this complexity, the Kubernetes ecosystem has produced a rich collection of complementary tools and
practices that make configuration management, packaging, and deployment easier, safer, and more reproducible.
Among them, three have become particularly popular: GitOps, Helm 3, and Kustomize.
Let's take a brief look at each.
GitOps: Declarative delivery through version control
Kubernetes was built around the idea of declarative configuration—you describe the desired end state of your
system, and the platform ensures that this state is achieved and maintained. GitOps takes i d x _ 1 e 2 8 3 a 4 1 this principle one step
further by applying it to the entire operational life cycle of a cluster.
In a GitOps workflow, Git becomes the single source of truth for both your application code and your infrastructure
configuration. Every change to the cluster—whether it's a Deployment, a ConfigMap, or a network policy—is

represented as a commit in a Git repository. Automated agents running inside the cluster continuously monitor
that repository and reconcile any differences between what's declared in Git and what's actually running.
This approach has i d x _ 0 f f a a b 2 5 several powerful advantages:

25968.title: ultimatedockercontainerbookfourthedition
25968.heading: Chapter 15 516

Auditability: Every change to the cluster is recorded in Git history, making it easy to track who changed
what and when
Reproducibility: A new cluster can be bootstrapped directly from the same Git repository, guaranteeing
that environments stay consistent
Safety: Changes are applied only after being merged and reviewed, reducing human error and
configuration drift
Automation: Tools such as Argo CD and Flux automatically synchronize cluster state with Git, removing
the need for manual kubectl apply commands
GitOps represents a cultural as well as a technical shift: it merges development and operations practices by making
infrastructure management fully version-controlled, reviewable, and automated. It is now widely considered a
best practice for running production Kubernetes clusters.
Helm 3: The package manager for Kubernetes
If GitOps defines how we manage and deliver i d x _ 8 6 2 3 7 2 1 4 configuration, Helm helps us manage what we deliver. Helm is often
described as the package manager for Kubernetes—similar to apt on Ubuntu or brew on macOS—but instead of
system packages, Helm installs and manages Kubernetes resources.
A Helm package is called a chart. Each chart i d x _ 1 b 1 9 2 3 f 5 bundles together a set of Kubernetes manifests and associated
templates for deploying a specific application or component. Charts can define default values, environment-
specific overrides, dependencies, and life cycle hooks. Using Helm, complex applications can be installed with a
single command:
$ helm install my-app bitnami/nginx
Helm then renders the templates with the provided values, creates the necessary manifests, and applies them to
your cluster.
With Helm 3, the i d x _ f c e 2 7 f c f tool matured significantly. It removed the server-side component (Tiller) introduced in earlier
versions, simplifying security and operations. Helm 3 communicates directly with the Kubernetes API using your
local credentials, integrates seamlessly with RBAC, and supports signed charts for verifying authenticity.
The key benefits i d x _ 3 7 0 0 d b 0 8 of Helm include the following:
Simplicity: Install or upgrade entire applications with a single command
Reusability: Share charts across projects or teams and version them in repositories
Parameterization: Customize deployments easily through values files instead of editing raw YAML
Rollback: Revert to a previous release quickly if an update fails
Helm has become an integral part of modern Kubernetes operations, and most open source applications today
provide official Helm charts for instant deployment.

Kustomize: Native configuration customization
While Helm focuses on packaging and reusing application templates, Kustomize addresses i d x _ a 6 1 f 0 9 0 e a different challenge:
how to manage environment-specific differences without duplicating manifests. It allows you to customize
existing YAML files declaratively using overlays, patches, and variable substitutions, all without introducing a
separate templating language.
Kustomize works directly with plain Kubernetes YAML. You start with a base configuration (for example, your
application's Deployment and Service) and then define overlays for specific environments, such as staging or
production. Each overlay can modify only what differs—for instance, image tags, replica counts, or environment
variables—while the rest of the configuration is inherited from the base.
A simple example layout might look like this:
my-app/
├── base/
│ ├── deployment.yaml
│ ├── service.yaml
│ └── kustomization.yaml
└── overlays/
├── staging/
│ └── kustomization.yaml
└── production/
└── kustomization.yaml
To apply a particular overlay, you simply run the following:
$ kubectl apply -k overlays/staging/
Kustomize is i d x _ 8 6 5 a 8 9 f 5 now built directly into kubectl, which means you can use it without installing anything extra. This
makes it a lightweight yet powerful tool for managing variations across multiple environments while keeping your
i d x _ 7 1 a 5 5 b 2 e configuration DRY (Don't Repeat Yourself).
Bringing it all together
In practice, these tools are often used together. Helm or Kustomize handle the packaging and customization of
Kubernetes resources, while GitOps provides the automation layer that keeps clusters continuously aligned with
what's defined in Git. Together, they transform Kubernetes from a manual deployment engine into a fully
automated, declarative delivery platform.
As you continue your journey with Kubernetes, you will see these tools and practices appear repeatedly—not just
in small projects, but also in large-scale enterprise environments. They represent the next evolutionary step in
managing infrastructure as code: repeatable, auditable, and fully automated.

In this section, we introduced three of the most widely adopted tools in the Kubernetes ecosystem. GitOps i d x _ 4 0 7 a 4 0 c e extends
declarative management into a fully automated workflow driven by version control. Helm 3 i d x _ e 8 b 2 e 2 8 1 simplifies packaging
and deploying applications through reusable charts. Kustomize i d x _ d 6 3 3 b 9 b f enables clean, environment-specific configuration
without duplicating manifests.
Together, they embody the modern Kubernetes philosophy: automate everything, declare everything, and keep
everything under version control.

Answers
Here are some exemplary answers to the preceding questions:
Kubernetes solves the challenge of running containerized applications reliably and at scale. It
automatically schedules workloads, manages resources, and ensures that the desired number of
containers are always running. Unlike traditional manual deployments, Kubernetes uses a declarative
model and a control loop to reconcile desired and actual state continuously.
The main components of Kubernetes are the control plane (which includes the API server, controller
manager, scheduler, and etcd) and the worker nodes (which run Pods through the kubelet and container
runtime). The control plane makes global decisions about the cluster, while worker nodes execute those
decisions by running the workloads.
A Pod is the smallest deployable unit in Kubernetes. It can contain one or more tightly coupled containers
that share networking and storage. While Docker focuses on individual containers, Kubernetes Pods
group containers that need to communicate and operate together as a single unit.
Docker Desktop, minikube, and kind all run local Kubernetes clusters but differ in setup and purpose.
Docker Desktop provides the easiest integrated option for developers. minikube uses a lightweight VM or
container backend and supports add-ons for experimentation. kind runs entirely inside Docker
containers and is ideal for testing and CI/CD pipelines.
Declarative configuration means defining the desired end state of your application or infrastructure—for
example, how many replicas should exist or which image should be used—instead of giving step-by-step
commands. Kubernetes continuously ensures that the actual state matches this desired state, which
makes systems more predictable and self-healing.
GitOps applies declarative management to the entire delivery process. Configuration and deployments
are stored in Git, which becomes the single source of truth. Tools such as Argo CD or Flux continuously
reconcile the running cluster state with what's stored in Git, ensuring reproducibility, auditability, and
automation.
A Helm chart is a reusable package that bundles all Kubernetes manifests required to deploy an
application. Helm allows you to parameterize configurations, manage dependencies, and perform
upgrades or rollbacks with a single command, greatly simplifying application life cycle management.
Kustomize lets you modify existing YAML manifests declaratively using overlays and patches, without
introducing a separate templating language. This makes it ideal for maintaining multiple environments
(for example, development, staging, and production) while keeping configurations consistent and DRY.
Helm, Kustomize, and GitOps complement each other. Helm provides reusable packaging, Kustomize

So far, our application is up and running—but Kubernetes doesn't yet know how to tell whether our Pods are truly
healthy or ready to receive traffic. If the API process hangs or if a container starts slowly, Kubernetes will simply
assume everything is fine.
In the next section, we'll fix that by defining liveness, readiness, and startup probes. These probes allow Kubernetes
to monitor the internal state of your application, restart containers when they become unhealthy, and delay traffic
routing until they're ready to serve requests.
Defining liveness, readiness, and startup probes
Kubernetes gives i d x _ a 4 0 9 a 3 8 e us powerful mechanisms to detect whether an application is healthy and ready to receive
requests. These mechanisms are called probes.
A probe is a small diagnostic check that the kubelet runs against a container to determine its state. The results are
reported back to Kubernetes, which then decides how to react. The three main types are listed next:
Liveness probe: Detects if a i d x _ 8 8 5 f a a c 8 container is still running properly. If it fails, Kubernetes restarts the
container.
Readiness probe: Detects i d x _ d f 1 8 2 b 5 4 if a container is ready to serve traffic. If it fails, Kubernetes temporarily
removes the Pod from the Service's endpoints.
Startup probe: Used i d x _ e 2 0 4 1 3 f 3 for containers that take a long time to initialize. It delays liveness and readiness
checks until the startup completes.
By defining these probes, we allow Kubernetes to react automatically when things go wrong—for example, when
the API process hangs, or when the application is still starting up and should not yet receive traffic.

How rolling updates work
When you i d x _ c 4 e d b 8 6 5 update a Deployment in Kubernetes—for example, by changing the container image tag—Kubernetes
does not replace all i d x _ f 7 8 f 6 3 1 a existing Pods at once.
Instead, it does the following:
Creates new Pods based on the updated specification.
Waits for them to become ready (using the readiness probe we defined earlier).
Gradually terminates the old Pods as new ones take over.
This rolling behavior ensures that there are always enough healthy Pods available to serve traffic during the
update.
Let's experience this with a hands-on example.
Hands-on rolling update

The rbac-api.yaml file i d x _ 0 5 5 c 4 7 9 e defines i d x _ b 6 c 4 4 8 8 2 the identity and permissions that the TaskBoard API Pods use when they run inside

Summary
In this chapter, we took everything we've learned about Kubernetes and applied it to a complete, realistic
application—TaskBoard.
We started by deploying a multi-service stack consisting of a database, backend API, and web frontend. We then
introduced probes to give Kubernetes visibility into application health, and saw how the platform can self-heal
automatically when something fails.
Next, we performed zero-downtime deployments, first using rolling updates and then blue-green deployments,
ensuring that new versions of our application can be released safely without interrupting users.
Finally, we focused on security best practices, running containers as non-root, applying the principle of least
privilege through RBAC, enforcing Pod security, restricting network traffic with NetworkPolicies, and handling
Secrets more safely.
With these building blocks in place, we now have a Kubernetes environment that is not only functional but also
resilient, secure, and ready for real-world use.
So far, we've worked entirely with local clusters. In the next chapter, we'll move beyond local development and
learn how to run containerized applications in the cloud.

Answers
Once you've worked through the questions, compare your responses with the answers that follow. Each
explanation expands slightly on the concept to clarify not just what is correct, but why—solidifying your grasp of
how Kubernetes maintains, updates, and secures containerized applications:
Readiness and liveness probes allow Kubernetes to monitor the health of your application containers. A
readiness probe determines if a container is ready to serve traffic; Pods failing this check are temporarily
removed from load balancing. A liveness probe detects if a container is still functioning properly; if it
fails, Kubernetes automatically restarts the container. These probes help ensure HA and self-healing
behavior without manual intervention.
A rolling update gradually replaces old Pods with new ones, ensuring the application stays available
throughout the update. A blue-green deployment runs two complete environments (old and new) in
parallel and switches traffic from one to the other in a single step.
The Deployment resource manages ReplicaSets, which in turn ensure that the desired number of Pod
replicas are running at all times. If a Pod fails, the Deployment automatically replaces it.
You can simulate a failure by killing one of the running Pods (for example, kubectl exec <pod> -- kill
1) and watch how the ReplicaSet immediately creates a new replacement Pod. Using kubectl get pods
-w, you'll see the terminated Pod disappear and a new one start within seconds, demonstrating
Kubernetes' self-healing mechanism.
Running as non-root limits the impact of a potential compromise. If an attacker gains access to the
container, they won't have administrative privileges on the node or cluster. It also aligns with Pod
Security Standards and is often required in enterprise clusters where Pod Security Admission is enforced.
A ServiceAccount defines an identity for processes running inside Pods. Through RBAC, you can assign
specific permissions to that identity—for example, allowing it to read ConfigMaps or Secrets. This
practice enforces the principle of least privilege, ensuring that each component can only access what it

Secrets mounted as files are read directly from memory-backed volumes and are less likely to appear in

Kubernetes uses the Deployment's rolling update strategy parameters (maxSurge and maxUnavailable)

monitoring, backup, and compliance mechanisms.
Setting up and maintaining such a production-grade Kubernetes cluster on your own infrastructure is a significant
challenge. You must provision and patch the underlying virtual machines (VMs), configure i d x _ d c 7 f c 4 2 b networking, handle
security updates, set i d x _ 0 c 2 5 f a 4 6 up high availability (HA), and i d x _ b a 4 8 8 5 2 2 ensure business continuity (BC). This is where the cloud

(EKS), Microsoft Azure Kubernetes Service (AKS), and Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE), that take i d x _ 8 e 1 2 0 2 1 c away most

-f ./api/Dockerfile \

Why choose a hosted Kubernetes service?
Running Kubernetes i d x _ d d 7 b 0 d 6 c yourself is an educational and empowering experience. In the previous chapters, we used
minikube, kind, and Docker Desktop to create and manage our own clusters locally. These setups help us
understand the core Kubernetes concepts and how all components work together. However, building and
maintaining a production-grade Kubernetes cluster in a real-world environment is a different story altogether.
Operating Kubernetes at scale involves a long list of complex and time-consuming tasks. You must provision and
configure VMs, set up and maintain the control plane, manage certificates, monitor the health of cluster
components, configure networking and load balancers, and apply security patches regularly. On top of that, you

must ensure that your cluster is resilient, scalable, and compliant with your company's governance standards. All
of this requires deep expertise, dedicated operations staff, and continuous attention.
To address these challenges, all major cloud providers, such as i d x _ 8 e 5 1 e 5 1 7 AWS, Microsoft Azure, and Google Cloud
Platform (GCP), offer i d x _ 6 a 5 4 d 0 a c fully managed Kubernetes services. These services take care of most of the operational heavy
lifting by managing the control plane for you, providing integrated monitoring, security, and scaling features out of

Some key advantages i d x _ 8 4 1 2 7 2 d 5 of using a managed Kubernetes service are as follows:
Simplified cluster management: The cloud provider provisions and maintains the Kubernetes control
plane, applies patches, and ensures HA and reliability.
Integrated security and identity management: Managed services integrate seamlessly with the

guarantee fault tolerance (FT) and i d x _ 4 d 1 c b c 4 1 minimize downtime.

monitoring, and CI/CD tools.

managing infrastructure, patching clusters, or troubleshooting control-plane i d x _ 6 3 5 2 5 e c 4 issues.

grade reliability and scalability. They enable organizations to adopt Kubernetes more quickly, minimize
operational complexity, and accelerate their journey toward modern, cloud-native architectures.

Cost and responsibility
While managed Kubernetes i d x _ 4 9 4 4 d 6 5 2 services simplify operations, they do not eliminate all i d x _ d 0 1 2 9 f e 9 responsibilities. Cloud providers
typically manage the control plane, including the API server, scheduler, and etcd database, while users remain
responsible for their worker nodes, workloads, and application-level configurations. You are still accountable for
security within your cluster, such as implementing RBAC policies, managing secrets, defining network rules, and
keeping your application images free from vulnerabilities.
From a cost perspective, you pay for two things: the managed control plane (which is usually billed per hour or per
cluster) and the worker nodes, which are charged as regular VMs. Although running Kubernetes in the cloud may
appear more expensive at first glance, the operational savings and the improved reliability often outweigh the
infrastructure costs. For most organizations, the trade-off between cost and reduced maintenance effort is well
worth it.
In the following sections, we will explore how to deploy a simple containerized application to three of the most
popular managed Kubernetes services: EKS, AKS, and GKE.
Overview of the managed Kubernetes services covered
in this chapter
The next three sections will i d x _ 5 7 8 9 0 0 7 4 demonstrate how to deploy the same simple containerized application to three of the
most popular managed Kubernetes services: EKS, AKS, and GKE. Although all three offerings are based on the same
open source Kubernetes foundation, each provider has developed its own philosophy and tooling around it.
Amazon EKS emphasizes i d x _ f 7 4 e 5 7 e c integration with the AWS ecosystem, focusing on security and fine-grained identity
management through IAM. Azure AKS provides i d x _ e d 4 5 8 f 4 1 a deeply integrated experience with Azure Active Directory, ACR,
and other native Azure resources. Google GKE, on the other i d x _ 2 6 0 b 8 5 c 7 hand, remains the most mature Kubernetes
implementation, as Kubernetes itself originated at Google. It offers sophisticated automation features, such as
cluster auto-repair, auto-upgrades, and an optional fully managed mode called Autopilot.
In the following sections, we will briefly review each of these managed services, create a small cluster, and deploy a
simple multi-tier application to it. While the setup commands differ slightly, the Kubernetes i d x _ 2 9 5 f 1 9 3 3 manifests and
deployment principles remain the same, demonstrating the true portability and consistency of Kubernetes across
cloud environments.

managed by AWS, allowing you to focus on your workloads rather than maintaining Kubernetes i d x _ 1 a d 5 8 5 2 f itself. EKS

Serverless containers and the future of cloud-native
architectures
Over the past few years, cloud computing has continued to evolve. After VMs and containers came orchestration
platforms such as Kubernetes. Now, the industry is gradually shifting toward serverless containers, where
infrastructure management fades entirely into the background.
The principle remains the same: package your application and its dependencies into a container image. The
difference lies in how that container is run. With serverless containers, there are no visible nodes, clusters, or
instance groups to manage. You simply provide the image, specify how much CPU and memory it needs, and let the
cloud provider handle scheduling, scaling, networking, and availability.
Let's look at how each major cloud provider implements this concept.

AWS Fargate
AWS Fargate is the i d x _ b f c 0 7 9 0 1 serverless compute engine for containers on AWS. It works with both Amazon ECS and Amazon
EKS.
With Fargate, there are no EC2 instances to manage. Each pod (on EKS) or task (on ECS) runs in its own isolated
runtime environment. AWS provisions and scales the underlying infrastructure automatically.
From a developer's perspective, running on Fargate means the following:
No node groups or autoscaling groups to manage
No patching or capacity planning
Pay-per-use pricing based on CPU and memory consumed per second
Fargate integrates deeply with IAM, CloudWatch, and VPC networking, making it ideal for production workloads
that benefit from strong security isolation and simplified operations. You can think of it as Kubernetes without the
cluster management overhead.
Google Cloud Run
Google Cloud Run takes i d x _ 9 8 8 f 0 7 7 e serverless containers even further. Built on top of open standards (Knative), Cloud Run
allows you to run any stateless container directly, without dealing with Kubernetes resources at all. You provide a
container image, and Cloud Run automatically handles scaling from zero to thousands of instances based on
incoming HTTP traffic.
Each Cloud Run service has the following attributes:
Is fully managed and billed per request and execution time
Scales to zero when idle (no cost while unused)
Can be deployed from any OCI-compliant image (Docker Hub, Artifact Registry, etc.)
Supports custom domains, HTTPS, and fine-grained IAM permissions
Cloud Run blurs the line i d x _ 4 2 5 2 c 6 3 c between function-as-a-service (FAAS) and container orchestration, offering the best of
both worlds: the flexibility of containers with the operational simplicity of serverless.
Azure Container Apps
On the i d x _ f 0 2 d 4 0 5 d Microsoft side, Azure Container Apps (ACA) is the serverless container platform that builds i d x _ f 8 9 4 4 1 f 1 on Kubernetes
and the open source Kubernetes Event-driven Autoscaling (KEDA) project.
Like Cloud Run, it abstracts away the cluster and infrastructure, letting you run microservices, APIs, or background
workers directly from container images.
Key benefits i d x _ 4 4 6 5 b 6 d 4 include the following:
Autoscaling based on HTTP traffic, queue depth, or custom metrics
Built-in integration with Azure Monitor and Dapr for event-driven communication
Secure networking via i d x _ f f f 2 6 f c 5 Azure Virtual Networks (VNets)
Support for i d x _ 8 7 3 c 1 5 8 a revision-based deployments and rollbacks
ACA provides a seamless path for teams familiar with AKS but seeking a fully managed, scale-to-zero experience.

A ClusterIP Service exposes a workload only within the cluster's internal network, suitable for
communication between Pods (for example, between the API and the database). A LoadBalancer Service
provisions an external cloud load balancer, exposing the application publicly and assigning it an external

A StatefulSet preserves pod identity and stable storage, ensuring that each database instance has a

Disabling service links prevents Kubernetes from automatically injecting environment variables for all

They remove the need to manage Kubernetes clusters or nodes entirely. Developers only provide a
container image and runtime parameters, and the platform automatically scales, runs, and manages the
container, charging only for actual usage. This simplifies operations while preserving the flexibility of
containers.
Serverless containers are ideal for stateless, event-driven, or bursty workloads where demand fluctuates
heavily or where managing cluster infrastructure adds unnecessary complexity. Traditional Kubernetes

In the previous chapter, we deployed our containerized application to the cloud and verified that it was running
successfully. We saw how orchestration platforms such as Kubernetes handle scaling, load balancing, and rolling
updates to keep workloads healthy. However, deployment is not the finish line; it's the beginning of the
operational journey. Once an application is live, the focus shifts from getting it to run to keeping it running reliably.
Running an application in production requires more than robust infrastructure; it demands visibility. Without
insight into what's happening inside the system, troubleshooting becomes guesswork, and small issues can
quickly escalate into outages. This is where observability comes in: the discipline of collecting and analyzing
signals that describe the internal state of a system based on its external outputs.
In this chapter, we will explore how to instrument, monitor, and troubleshoot a containerized application running
in production. We begin by adding OpenTelemetry (OTel) instrumentation to our services to trace requests across
multiple components, giving us full end-to-end visibility into system behavior. We then extend observability with
Prometheus and Grafana, collecting and visualizing key metrics that describe application health and performance.
Building on this foundation, we define alerts and create runbooks that turn raw telemetry into actionable
operational insight. Finally, we close the loop by learning how to review, test, and continuously improve our
monitoring setup to maintain operational readiness as the system evolves.
Together, these practices transform production monitoring from reactive troubleshooting into a proactive
discipline: one that helps you detect issues early, understand their impact, and respond quickly and confidently
when things go wrong.

Best practices for instrumentation
When i d x _ c 5 8 5 6 1 3 b instrumenting your services with OpenTelemetry, a few guiding principles help ensure that the resulting
observability data remains consistent, actionable, and future-proof:
Instrument early: Introduce telemetry at the start of development, not after issues appear.
Standardize service naming: Consistent naming enables coherent dashboards and traces.
Include business context: Beyond technical metrics, record user or transaction identifiers where
appropriate.
Correlate metrics and traces: Link latency spikes with trace spans for quick diagnosis.
Export in OTLP: Prefer OTLP for maximum interoperability.
Wrapping it up
In this section, we introduced OpenTelemetry, the modern standard for unified observability. You learned how to
instrument your services, deploy the OpenTelemetry Collector, and visualize request traces using Jaeger. With
these foundations in place, every request in your distributed application can now be traced from end to end,
providing invaluable insight into its behavior under real workloads.

With both tracing and metrics in place, you have two of the three pillars of observability.

Defining alerts and runbooks
When i d x _ b 7 6 a 6 1 a 1 observability is done right, it doesn't stop at dashboards. Visualizations help you understand trends, but
alerts ensure you act when systems deviate from normal. An alert transforms metrics into a i d x _ 8 5 1 1 e 5 0 6 human or automated
response, bridging the gap between knowing and doing. Yet, an alert without guidance is only half useful. That's
why every alert should have a corresponding runbook: a concise, actionable set of instructions describing what to
check, what might have caused the issue, and how to resolve it.
In this section, we define alert rules in Prometheus, connect them to Alertmanager for routing and notification, and
finally complement them with simple runbooks for the most critical scenarios in our demo application.
635 Monitoring and Troubleshooting an Application Running in Production
Understanding the purpose of alerts
An alert i d x _ f 7 a 5 4 1 8 5 should draw attention only when something requires action. Not every deviation from the baseline
deserves a page or a Slack message. The best alerts are predictive, not reactive: they warn about a trend that will
soon lead to user impact rather than one that already has.
At their core, alerts are i d x _ 7 e a e e 0 c b simply PromQL expressions evaluated at regular intervals. When a condition remains true
for a defined duration, Prometheus fires the alert. This mechanism allows you to define conditions such as error

However, beyond i d x _ 9 a 7 4 a 3 d e the technical expression lies an operational principle: alert fatigue is worse than missing a
single event. Too many noisy alerts lead to apathy; too few mean blind spots. The goal is to achieve a balance, alert
on symptoms of real user pain, and rely on dashboards and logs for diagnosis.
To keep alerts effective, follow three guiding ideas:
Alert on symptoms, not causes. Users care about slow responses, not which container ran out of CPU.
Define clear ownership. Every alert must have a team or individual responsible for handling it.
Include context. A good alert message provides a link to a dashboard or runbook entry so that the
responder can act quickly.
In the following subsection, we'll define Prometheus alerting rules for our orders-service and payments-service,
focusing on two primary conditions—high error rate and elevated latency—and learn how to connect them to
Alertmanager for notification routing.
Defining alert rules in Prometheus
Prometheus i d x _ 9 6 a 8 5 5 e 2 can do more than collect and store metrics—it i d x _ 0 c 0 9 0 a 1 9 can evaluate expressions and raise alerts whenever
certain conditions are met. These alerts are defined as part of alerting rule groups, which Prometheus periodically
evaluates. When a rule's expression is true for a specified duration, Prometheus marks the alert as firing and sends
it to Alertmanager for routing.
Alert rules are defined in a separate YAML file, typically loaded through a ConfigMap and referenced by
i d x _ 5 7 e a 3 8 f 1 Prometheus in its configuration. This allows rules to be versioned, deployed, and reloaded independently of the
Prometheus binary.
A minimal i d x _ 6 e 6 9 7 f e 2 alerting configuration looks like this:
groups:
- name: service_alerts
interval: 30s
rules:
- alert: HighErrorRate
expr: rate(orders_errors_total[2m]) /
rate(orders_requests_total[2m]) > 0.05
for: 1m
labels:
severity: warning

Connecting Prometheus to Alertmanager
Prometheus is i d x _ d d 0 8 4 c 6 e responsible for detecting and i d x _ 8 e 4 6 6 e 9 4 firing alerts, but it is not designed to manage notifications or
escalation policies. That's the role of Alertmanager, a companion service that receives alerts from Prometheus,
groups related ones together, suppresses duplicates, and routes them to the right communication channels such as
email, Slack, Microsoft Teams, or PagerDuty.
The integration between Prometheus and Alertmanager is straightforward—Prometheus sends all active alerts to
one or more Alertmanager instances via a small configuration block in prometheus.yml:
alerting:
alertmanagers:
- static_configs:
639 Monitoring and Troubleshooting an Application Running in Production
- targets:
- "alertmanager.observability.svc.cluster.local:9093"
This line tells Prometheus where to deliver its alerts. The corresponding Alertmanager instance listens on port 9093
and processes all incoming notifications.
Alertmanager itself is configured through a separate YAML file, commonly called alertmanager.yml. Here, you
define routes, receivers, and optional inhibition rules. A minimal setup that sends notifications to both email and
Slack might look like this:
global:
resolve_timeout: 5m
route:
receiver: default
group_by: ['alertname', 'service']
group_wait: 10s
group_interval: 1m
repeat_interval: 2h
receivers:
- name: default
email_configs:
- to: "ops@example.com"
from: "alertmanager@example.com"
smarthost: "smtp.example.com:587"
auth_username: "alertmanager@example.com"
auth_identity: "alertmanager@example.com"
auth_password: "your-password"
slack_configs:
- api_url: "https://hooks.slack.com/services/your/webhook/url"
channel: "#alerts"
title: "{{ .CommonAnnotations.summary }}"
text: "{{ .CommonAnnotations.description }}"
This i d x _ a b 5 0 4 d d 7 configuration defines a single route i d x _ 7 3 9 a 6 a b d named default that groups alerts by name and service, waits briefly
before sending the first notification (group_wait), and repeats only if the alert remains active after two hours.
Two receivers are specified: one sends an email, and the other posts to a Slack channel using an incoming
webhook.

Creating practical runbooks
An alert i d x _ c c c c a 8 b a by itself is just a signal. What makes it operationally valuable is the context it provides, the knowledge of
what to do next. That's where runbooks come in. A i d x _ e 2 4 8 f f a b runbook is a concise, structured document that tells the
responder exactly how to investigate and resolve the condition that triggered the alert.
Runbooks close the gap between detection and resolution. They ensure that whoever is on call, whether an
experienced engineer or a newcomer, can respond confidently and consistently. In modern teams, runbooks are
often stored alongside the code base or linked directly from alerts and dashboards, making them easy to maintain
and evolve.
A well-written runbook entry typically contains the following:
Summary: A short description of the alert or issue
Impact: What this condition means for users or systems
Immediate checks: The first actions to confirm or rule out the issue
Potential causes: Common reasons why this alert might fire
Remediation steps: What to do to mitigate or fix the problem

Check recent i d x _ 1 3 7 5 d b 5 7 application logs for stack traces or connection errors.

Restart affected pods if the error appears transient.
